segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: greatly annoyed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they seized them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes assembled in Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: together with Annas the high priest, and Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who belonged to the high-priestly family.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They had them stand in the middle and began to question them:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “By what power or in what name did you do this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rulers of the people and elders,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: if we are being examined today about a good deed done to a disabled man, and by what means this man has been made well,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man stands before you healthy.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He is the stone that was scorned by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And salvation is in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seeing the boldness of Peter and John, and realizing that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they were amazed, and they recognized that they had been with Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And seeing the man who had been healed standing with them, they had nothing to say in reply.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they ordered them to go outside the council and conferred with one another,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are we to do with these men? For that a notable sign has taken place through them is plain to everyone living in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But so that it spreads no further among the people, let us threaten them not to speak any longer in this name to anyone at all.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they called them in and ordered them not to utter a word or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter and John answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After threatening them further, they released them, finding no way to punish them because of the people, since everyone was glorifying God for what had happened;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the man on whom this sign of healing had been done was more than forty years old.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After they were released, they went to their own people and reported everything the chief priests and the elders had said to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard it, they raised their voice to God with one accord and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Master, you who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: who said by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant: ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot empty things?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Messiah.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For truly in this city there gathered against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: to do everything that your hand and your plan had determined beforehand should happen.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your slaves to speak your word with all boldness,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders take place through the name of your holy servant Jesus.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking the word of God with boldness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the whole body of those who believed was one in heart and soul, and not one of them said that anything he owned was his own, but they held everything in common.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With great power the apostles kept giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there was no one in need among them, because all who were owners of lands or houses would sell them and bring the proceeds of what was sold

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and lay them at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each according to what anyone needed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, which translated means Son of Encouragement, a Levite, a Cypriot by birth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: sold a field that belonged to him, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

notes.note: This was a senior priestly official responsible for order in the temple precincts and for its Levite police. He was a Jewish officer, not a Roman one, and is commonly identified with the official whom later Jewish sources rank next to the high priest.

Annas had held the office years earlier (about AD 6–15) before being removed by the Roman governor. The serving high priest at this time was his son-in-law Caiaphas. Luke gives Annas the title anyway, as in Luke 3:2, probably reflecting his continuing authority as head of the dominant high-priestly family. The John and Alexander named here are otherwise unknown.

notes.traditional: is made whole / has been healed
notes.note: The Greek verb covers both healing and rescue. It is the same verb translated “saved” in verse 12, where the related noun is “salvation.” Peter's speech moves deliberately from the man's cure to salvation in the widest sense, and English needs two words where Greek has one.

Peter adapts Psalm 118:22, sharpening “rejected” to “scorned” and adding “by you.” The Greek is literally “head of the corner,” which may be a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the final stone that crowns a wall or arch. Scholars are divided; either way it is the stone on which the structure depends.

The first word often means “illiterate” in documents of the period, but here it most likely means that they lacked formal training in the Law such as scribes had. The second word (idiōtēs) means a layperson, someone without professional or official standing, and does not imply stupidity. The council's surprise is that men without credentials speak so confidently.

This word is elsewhere rendered “righteous” or “just.” Here it stands in the ordinary Greek idiom “it is right to do something,” where neither of those is natural English. Nearly all translations have “right.”

This is not the usual word for “Lord,” which appears in verse 29. It is the term for the master of a household or the owner of slaves, and it was used in prayer, including in the Septuagint, for God as absolute ruler. It matches the believers' description of themselves as “slaves” in verse 29.

notes.phrase: who said by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant
notes.traditional: who by the mouth of thy servant David hast said
notes.note: The Greek of the earliest manuscripts is grammatically tangled here, with “of our father,” “through the Holy Spirit” and “by the mouth of David” piled together. Many scholars suspect a very early copying error. Later manuscripts have a shorter, smoother form without “our father” and “the Holy Spirit,” which older English versions follow. The translation gives the probable sense of the earlier text.

The quotation is Psalm 2:1–2. One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples, so “the nations” is equally possible in the psalm itself. “Gentiles” is used because verse 27 applies the psalm term by term, with the same word for the Romans alongside “the peoples of Israel,” and Herod and Pilate as the kings and rulers.

The Greek christos means “anointed one” and is the word English borrows as “Christ.” In the psalm it is a title for God's anointed king, so “Messiah” is used here, as in several modern translations; others have “his Anointed.” The prayer picks the word up at once: “whom you anointed” in verse 27 is the related verb.

The Greek word can mean either “child” or “servant.” It is the same word used of David in verse 25, and the Septuagint uses it for the servant of the Lord in Isaiah. Most modern translations and scholars read “servant” here; “child” is the older English rendering.

This is the ordinary word for a slave, a person who belongs to a master. It is a different word from the one translated “servant” in verses 25, 27 and 30. In the Septuagint it is also an honourable way of describing those who belong wholly to God. Most English translations soften it to “servants.”

The Greek noun covers encouragement, exhortation and comfort, so “son of consolation” or “son of exhortation” is also possible. “Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone marked by a quality. How the name Barnabas yields this meaning in Aramaic is uncertain and debated.

candidates.reason: One verb covers healing and salvation, often with deliberate double meaning, and translators need a consistent policy for when to split it and how to flag the link.
It recurs throughout the New Testament, and the choice between “slave” and the traditional “servant” changes how readers hear both social relationships and believers' relation to God.
It can mean child or servant; it is used of Jesus and David in Acts 3–4 with Isaianic overtones, and should be kept distinct from δοῦλος and from words for son or child.
It is a key term in Acts, John, Paul and Hebrews, variously rendered boldness, confidence, openness and plainness, and readers lose the thread if the English varies.
Translations alternate between “council” and the loanword “Sanhedrin” across the Gospels and Acts, and one decision is needed.
